course.title: C++ Programming Foundations
course.shortDescription: Learn C++ from zero — variables, control flow, functions, pointers, and object-oriented programming — with real compiled code challenges graded automatically.
course.longDescription:
This showcase course follows the freeCodeCamp C++ Tutorial for Beginners curriculum by Mike Dane, split into focused video segments. Between segments you will solve real C++ challenges that compile and run on the Mentrily judge — with public and hidden test cases, exactly like a technical interview platform.

You will finish able to read and write idiomatic beginner C++: typed variables, strings and numeric operations, conditionals and loops, functions with return values, pointers, and classes with constructors, getters/setters, and inheritance.
course.courseSummary: C++ toolchain setup, variables and data types, strings and numbers, user input, arrays, functions, if/switch statements, while/for loops, 2D arrays, pointers, classes and objects, constructors, getters/setters, inheritance.

content.description: Install a C++ toolchain, understand the anatomy of a C++ program, and print your first output.
content.problemStatement: Install a C++ toolchain, understand the anatomy of a C++ program, and print your first output.

contentBlocks.content:
Why C++ still runs the world

C++ is a compiled, statically-typed language: your source code is translated ahead of time into machine code, and every variable's type is checked before the program ever runs. That is why C++ powers game engines, operating systems, trading systems, and embedded devices — and why learning it teaches you how computers actually work.

Every C++ program you write in this course has the same skeleton:

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    cout << "Hello, Mentrily!" << endl;
    return 0;
}
  • Watch for: what #include and using namespace std actually do
  • Watch for: why execution always starts at main()

Note: you don't need to install anything locally — every challenge in this course compiles and runs right in your browser on the Mentrily judge.

content.description: The core data types, string operations, and the math toolkit.
content.problemStatement: The core data types, string operations, and the math toolkit.

contentBlocks.content:
Types are promises

In C++ a variable's type is a promise to the compiler: int holds whole numbers, double holds decimals, char holds a single character, string holds text, and bool holds true/false. Break the promise and the compiler refuses to build your program — which is a feature, not an annoyance: it catches bugs before they exist.

  • Watch for: integer division — 10 / 4 is 2, not 2.5
  • Watch for: string methods like .length(), .find(), and .substr()
  • Watch for: the cmath functions pow, sqrt, round

Read a single number (Celsius, possibly decimal) from standard input and print the Fahrenheit equivalent rounded to one decimal place.

content.description: Reading user input, storing collections in arrays, and organizing code into functions with return values.
content.problemStatement: Reading user input, storing collections in arrays, and organizing code into functions with return values.

contentBlocks.content:
Programs that respond

Real programs consume input. cin >> reads whitespace-separated values; getline() reads whole lines. Arrays store fixed-size collections (int scores[5]), and functions carve programs into named, reusable pieces. The key discipline: a function should do one thing, take what it needs as parameters, and hand back its result with return — not print it.

  • Watch for: the calculator and Mad Libs projects — input in action
  • Watch for: why functions must be declared before main() uses them (or prototyped)

content.description: if/else chains, comparison and logical operators, switch statements, while and for loops — the decision-making core of every program.
content.problemStatement: if/else chains, comparison and logical operators, switch statements, while and for loops — the decision-making core of every program.

contentBlocks.content:
Decisions and repetition

Everything a computer does reduces to decide and repeat. This segment covers if / else if / else with the comparison (==, !=, >, <=) and logical (&&, ||, !) operators, switch for multi-way branches, and both loop styles: while (loop until a condition changes) and for (loop a known number of times).

  • Watch for: the guessing-game project combining a while loop with if statements
  • Watch for: the classic bug — = (assignment) where == (comparison) was intended
  • Watch for: why a missing break makes switch cases "fall through"

content.description: Grids of data with nested loops, then the concept that defines C++: pointers and memory addresses.
content.problemStatement: Grids of data with nested loops, then the concept that defines C++: pointers and memory addresses.

contentBlocks.content:
Where variables actually live

Every variable occupies a numbered slot in memory — its address. A pointer is simply a variable that stores an address. Two operators do all the work: &x gives you the address of x, and *p dereferences a pointer to reach the value stored at that address.

int age = 25;
int *p = &age;   // p holds the address of age
cout << *p;      // prints 25 — the value at that address

Understanding pointers is understanding how arrays, strings, and objects are passed around under the hood — it is the concept interviewers probe hardest.

  • Watch for: nested loops walking a 2D array row by row
  • Watch for: the difference between a pointer and the value it points to

content.title: Dereference trace
content.question: int x = 10; int *p = &x; *p = 99; — what is x now?
content.description:
int x = 10;
int *p = &x;
*p = 99;
cout << x;

What does this print?
content.problemStatement:
int x = 10;
int *p = &x;
*p = 99;
cout << x;

What does this print?

options.text: 10 — p is a copy, x is unchanged
Undefined behavior — p was never allocated

content.description: Bundling data and behavior: classes, constructors, object functions, getters/setters, and inheritance.
content.problemStatement: Bundling data and behavior: classes, constructors, object functions, getters/setters, and inheritance.

contentBlocks.content:
Objects: data + behavior, together

A class is a blueprint: it declares the data an object holds (attributes) and the operations it supports (methods). A constructor runs at creation to initialize state; getters and setters guard access to private attributes; and inheritance lets a derived class reuse and specialize a base class.

class Book {
  private:
    string title;
  public:
    Book(string t) { title = t; }      // constructor
    string getTitle() { return title; } // getter
};
  • Watch for: why attributes default to private and what public: changes
  • Watch for: the inheritance example — a derived class overriding a base method

Course complete — exam ahead

That covers the full four-hour curriculum. The final exam has 10 concept questions (types, control flow, pointers, OOP) and one compiled coding challenge with hidden test cases. You need 75% and have 2 attempts. Re-run the three challenges in this course before attempting it.

content.title: Challenge: Bank Account Class
content.question: Complete a BankAccount class with deposit/withdraw methods, then process a list of transactions.
content.description:
Complete the BankAccount class. Input format:

starting_balance
N
op amount   (N lines: op is D for deposit or W for withdraw)

Withdrawals that exceed the balance must be ignored. After processing all transactions, print the final balance (integer).

Example: start 100, transactions D 50, W 30, W 200 → prints 120 (the 200 withdrawal is ignored).
content.problemStatement: Complete the BankAccount class (deposit, withdraw that ignores overdrafts, getBalance), then read a starting balance and N transactions (D amount / W amount) and print the final balance.
